patient_information: A 34-year-old man from Phuket, Thailand, presented to a hospital in Germany.
chief_complaint: The patient presented with a 2-week history of fever and a papular rash affecting his whole body.
history_of_present_illness: The patient had a 2-week history of fever, a papular rash on his face and trunk, and reported 7 kg weight loss in the last 3 months.
exposure_and_epidemiology: He lives in Thailand and arrived in Germany 3 days prior to visiting friends; Talaromycosis is caused by Talaromyces marneffei, a fungus endemic to East and Southeast Asia.
vitals: On examination, the patient was febrile with a temperature of 38.2°C (100.76°F).
physical_exam: The patient had pale conjunctivae, was very wasted with a BMI of 14 kg/m², a generalized non-pruritic rash of small umbilicated papules on his face and trunk, generalized lymphadenopathy with swollen lymph nodes in the left supraclavicular, inguinal, and axillary regions, palpable spleen at two fingers below the left costal margin, and a liver span of 15cm in the midclavicular line.
labs_and_diagnostics: Full blood count showed WBC 2.1 ×10⁹/L, haemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, platelets 110 ×10⁹/L, and C-reactive protein 150 mg/L. An HIV test was positive, with a CD4 cell count of 2/µL. Blood cultures, fine needle aspirate of lymph node, and skin biopsy were performed, and histopathology of the lymph node biopsy showed multiple yeast-like structures. Cultures from blood, skin biopsy, and lymph node all grew Talaromyces (Penicillium) marneffei.
differential_diagnosis: Differential diagnoses considered included HIV, CMV and EBV infection, molluscum contagiosum (in HIV-infected individuals), disseminated tuberculosis, atypical mycobacteria infections, melioidosis, Bartonella spp. (bacillary angiomatosis), fungal infections (cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, talaromycosis), visceral leishmaniasis, lymphomas, and HHV-8-associated Castleman's disease.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient was started on a 2-week course of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B followed by oral itraconazole, and antiretroviral therapy (ART) was initiated. On 3-week follow-up, he was afebrile and gaining weight. Six months later, he presented with a recurrence of cervical lymphadenopathy, and an infection with atypical mycobacteria was found, interpreted as immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) of the unmasking type, with his CD4 count at 102/µL and viral load suppressed.
final_diagnosis: Talaromycosis (previously penicilliosis) and HIV infection with subsequent immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) due to atypical mycobacteria.
